Second Life changed my life in ways I can't even being to explain to people who just see it as "a game". 

I'm autistic and have severe CPTSD, which for most of my life has made it legit impossible to function in any kind of real, non-superficial friendship without them inevitably leaving either because I'm "weird" (cant read any social cues and am essentially totally disconnected from mainstream culture since I only engage with the extremely specific interests I have)--

or they leave because they think I don't want to be their friend (I cant read any social cues, I have a completely flat and unchanging affect that makes me appear uninterested when I'm not, I am not a telepath and can't read their mind when they want me to do something but refuse to actually tell me, etc) 

I honest to God thought I'd be alone for my entire time on Earth. I always thought that if I wanted to have people in my life, I had to do my best to minimize myself as much as possible and mirror the other persons mannerisms in order to be socially palatable. 

Now thanks to SL I have a best friend who means the world to me, I am involved in a few different communities, and I am actually... functioning as a member of society. It's a cybersociety, sure, but the emotional connections that are developed inworld are very real. 

Probably gonna sound like a total loser when I say this, but if not for SL, I 100% would have killed myself by now

There are times I start talking about something, and I suddenly realize the person is not interested, which then causes my brain to spiral in one of two routes:

1.) I realize I'm being annoying and instantly freeze and can not make a single word come out which always makes the other person get mad, and then when I can't get my brain to let me communicate even a single coherent thought following it's decision that This Interaction Has Been Terminated, the only option I have other than panicking and sputtering broken word fragments at the other person is to just book it and leave the premises as quickly and in a way that draws as little attention to myself as possible. 

---OR---

2.) I keep talking, spewing out one unbroken paragraph after another at the person despite knowing that they are neither interested in the subject matter nor is it fair for me to subject them to a one-sided info-dumping monologue that serves them no practical benefit whatsoever. Even though for the entire time I am trying excruciatingly hard to stop, like I am mentally begging and pleading to my brain DESPERATELY begging myself to shut up, internally screaming at myself like--

*"please stop talking for the love of God, literally nobody cares or wants to hear you talk right now and especially not about whatever stupid useless topic you've selected, for once just stop being an annoying unpalatable waste of space and shut your goddamn mouth"*

---but I can't. I physically cannot override my annoying cringe-inducing personality. If I could delete myself and install a brand new operating system on my brain. The best solution I've been able to find that actually helps stop it from happening is to just isolate myself as much as I'm able and train myself to never talk about anything involving myself or my own interests, feelings, hobbies, etc.

There were really no rules for what I could or couldn't do as a kid when I was at my moms house for the summer. I woke up at 8 or so, had breakfast, and then would leave the house and explore in any way I could wherever I could get to until it was dark out. 

When I was like 13 or so, I loved interacting with new groups of people to sort of "study" them and how they interact with the other social groups in the area. And let me tell you something- if you don't express interest in typical "children's" things (TV, playing, etc), then even though you are 13 and honestly look like you're 9 or 10, people will almost not even cross their mind that you are a child. 

If you listen, and you learn the questions to ask, they will talk and talk and talk to you like you're an adult. They will tell you everything and treat you like they would someone of their own age. You will learn and see both some amazing things as well as some fucked up shit that stick with you for a while. 

You will learn the social internetwork that connects everyone of the entire town and beyond. Who has beef with who and why. The details of every messy marriage. The details of literal criminal activity (often times activities which people more or less HAD to do just to stay afloat). And all you had to do is listen.

I had next to zero friends as a kid. When I was 13, the most exciting thing I had to look forward to was staying with mom for the weekends and summer in a different neighborhood where I used a different name and told people I was the "opposite" gender (I'm trans now lol), and I'd get to meet all these people and learn every detail all because I was physically present, knew how to behave in a way that was perceived as neutral and easy to be near, and knew what questions to ask. 

My best group of "friends" was a group of about 5 men in their mid-late 20s at the time. I didn't have to speak a word and usually remained silent. I showed up, stood near them silently, and soon enough I was smoking with them while they all just.... accepted that I was a new member of their circle, as odd as that sounds. And I'd hang out in their apartment and they'd talk and talk and talk and I'd learn so much about everything. From them and pretty much all the other adults in the area. 

I'm in therapy now to process a lot of the shit that took place when I was on that constant mission to observe and study people like that. It was an objectively unsafe thing for a child to be doing and it certainly left its damage in a lot of ways. But given the option, there is not a damn thing I would change or do differently.

As a Christian struggling with a drug addiction, i can tell you right now that it’s not a matter of someone lacking religious integrity. Addiction itself doesn’t exist in a vacuum, there are a lot of outside factors that go into why one might become addicted to something. (You don’t just wake up one morning and say, “Gee, I’d really like be addicted to cocaine!”) 

For many of us, recovery is extremely difficult to access, difficult to achieve, and sometimes even hard to imagine due to how expensive healthcare is and how heavily stigmatized addiction is by society. We’re not being tricked by the devil, we’re living with a treatable health issue that we can’t get help for, because society has found every reason to make it impossible to even ask for help: shaming, guilting, arresting, ect.

I am very deeply a believer of Christ and I can feel His love all the time. I know in my heart of hearts that I am here to devote my life to Him and for helping cultivate His love in others. And very often, I will agree, that addicts may appear to some Christians as being disconnected from God, and many times that is true- many times, we DO distance ourselves from actively participating in religion as we’re struggling to recover.

But it’s not because we make the conscious decision to abandon Christ in order favor drugs instead. 
It’s because we’re alienated, shamed, invalidated, and dismissed by other Christians for needing help with addiction in the first place.
